results.message: What happened among you in the century between Cyprian and Augustine?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
From 258 to 391, our own ordinary pastoral voice falls silent, as far as we have weighed what survives. Cyprian died on 14 September 258. Augustine was seized at Hippo in 391 and made a presbyter against his wishes. Possidius wrote: “The Catholics already knew the life and teaching of the holy Augustine, and they seized him. He was standing there among the people, feeling safe and unaware of what was about to happen... So they seized him and, as is the custom in such cases, brought him to the bishop to be ordained. They did this because all of them, with one accord, wanted it done and carried through. They demanded it with great eagerness and loud shouting, while he wept freely.”

Between those years, a hundred and thirty-three, we cannot give you our own bishops' pastoral teaching as we give you theirs. A handful of old sermons may come from those years. We have not weighed them yet, so we neither lean on them nor rule them out. This is not an edge of what we know, the way our own beginning and our own end are edges. It sits inside our own life. It is a silence in our own pastoral voice, not a period in which nothing happened. Things did happen then. Councils met, and laws were made, and the Donatist schism ran through exactly those years. We do not explain that the silence exists, and we do not fill it from a neighbouring communion's own record, even where that record runs through exactly those years.

glosses.plain_meaning: We are not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we say so out loud. We can stand in front of a bishop's own seat and refuse to go home.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, 'the people' names the congregation when it acts. They consent, they demand, and they elect -- unlike the flock, which is the congregation being cared for.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a passive congregation or a modern democratic electorate with formal voting rights. Neither is right. A corporate body whose consent and demand genuinely constitute a call to office, and which can be exerted disruptively, but which holds no procedural mechanism and can still be refused.
false_friend: a passive congregation with no real leverage over its own clergy
a modern democratic electorate, with a formal ballot and a fixed voting procedure

sourced_by.citation: Possidius of Calama, Sancti Augustini Vita Scripta a Possidio Episcopo (Life of Augustine), ed. and trans. Herbert T. Weiskotten (Princeton: Princeton University Press; London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1919)

glosses.plain_meaning: We argue hard, and we stay. Schism is the other thing: when arguing stops, and a new altar and a new bishop appear in the same town.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, schism means a split in the one church: someone leaves its clergy and people and sets up another altar. It is a tear, not a mere argument.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear denominational difference -- a normal, unremarkable feature of a plural religious landscape. We mean a tearing of a single body, with real consequences for standing, sacraments, and ordinary life in a town where both parties are present -- not one option among many, but the outcome we organize ourselves to avoid.
false_friend: a normal, unremarkable feature of a plural religious landscape, carrying no great weight

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted rather than Documented, because the corroborating text is an early compilation whose compiler is unnamed, and vendored scholarship argues over how it relates to Pontius. The details only Pontius gives (the trees, the comparison to Zacchaeus, the trembling fingers, the hand strengthened from above) carry Contested confidence, and Inferential-Thin where hagiographic convention shapes them. The two texts differ on who tied the cloths over Cyprian's eyes. Which clause of CF V7.4's Tier 3 definition governs when they conflict is an open governance question (Doc_09 SS8 item 7), and this story does not rest on it.

In the vendored English edition of Cyprian the Latin plebs occurs exactly three times, all inside the 19th-century American editor's own introductory and elucidatory prose, none inside Cyprian's own letters. Cyprian's Latin does use it: Hartel's letters carry plebs in running text, 89 whole-word occurrences with notes excluded, and letter 43 is headed CYPRIANVS PLEBI VNIVERSAE S. 'The people' is the English volume's own recurring rendering for the congregation as an acting body. It is a working handle, and whether plebs becomes the world word is not settled.

The vendored Weiskotten scan carries a single OCR artifact inside this quotation -- 'ancf' for 'and' -- reproduced here exactly as the scan gives it (matching this record's own text against the raw file precisely, per this step's own discipline), not silently corrected; modern_rendering gives the plain sense ('they demanded it...') rather than reproducing the artifact.

confidence.divergence_note: How this world characterizes its own opponents -- the Donatists specifically -- belongs to a later, separate step and this world's eventual Representative, not to this lexicon; this entry names the general concept only and does not characterize Donatism. This term also carries a live scholarly contest, of the type Application to this world, secondarily Historical scope. It runs over whether the heresy/schism distinction was as stable in this period as later usage implies, and how far the category describes a real ecclesial situation as against a polemical instrument used by the side that eventually prevailed. The North African case is the field's own central example. The entry does not present the distinction as a neutral technical taxonomy, and it does not settle whether the application of the category to rivals was accurate.

The chunk's own Key Sources section states this precisely rather than leaving it to inference: 'The underlying primary-source facts reach Documented. The synthesis -- that these constitute one named cross-phase gravity rather than two separate historical facts -- is this build's own reasoning, at Widely Accepted, and Doc_04 SS3 flags the divergence rather than upgrading it.' This term record IS that synthesis, so its own formation_confidence follows the synthesis's own rating, not the underlying quoted facts' rating. Doc_03 itself characterizes the pattern the same way: inferred from both bishops' conduct across more than one text, not a term either bishop names as such.
